assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, using the magic-wavelength idea to trap neutral atoms with negligible light shift, brought many atoms into a Lamb-Dicke regime and moved timekeeping to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. This is precision measurement at its most fundamental: a new standard of accuracy that opens tests of constants, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the second. From an atomic-physics viewpoint the idea is original, clear and has a very large measurable impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and realised the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's group drove the clock to extreme accuracy and stability, with comb-linked comparisons and many-body (spin-polarised fermion) clocks. Two laureates is a clean configuration. Other groups (e.g. Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Schiller) and the Hall-Hänsch comb background are not credited here; the 2005 prize already recognised combs.
assessment.maturity: Many independent labs operate lattice clocks, intercomparisons agree at the 1e-18 level and the CIPM redefinition roadmap is under way. Recognition is timely and not premature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to credit the theoretical magic-wavelength proposal separately from the first experimental clock; I am relying on recalled history rather than verified priority records.
Overlap with ion-clock work (Wineland, Rosenband) already honoured in 2012 may be argued.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into a precision instrument for gravimetry, gradiometry, rotation sensing, measurement of the fine-structure constant and tests of the equivalence principle. The measurement-limits theme is central. Conceptually significant, with demonstrated sensitivity and a growing instrument base, and a natural complement to the laser-cooling and BEC prizes.
assessment.attribution: Bordé supplied the theory of atom interferometry and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer; Pritchard demonstrated early atom-optics and interferometers with light and gratings; Kasevich (with Chu) realised the light-pulse interferometer and the precision gravimeter. Chu already holds a Nobel for laser cooling, and Chapman, Mueller, Rasel, Dalibard and others contributed, so allocation is contestable. The three names supplied are a plausible but not unique selection.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by many groups; field-deployable gravimeters exist, though large-baseline fundamental-physics tests and the equivalence-principle bounds are still evolving. Mature for the core technique.
uncertainties: Priority among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich and Chu-linked work is not settled by the supplied text.
Whether the ultimate impact (beyond sensor technology) is judged large enough for a physics prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed flat bands with correlated insulators and unconventional superconductivity in a tunable, clean platform, launching twistronics and moire materials. Important, original and with immediate, large impact across condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle (2011); Jarillo-Herrero's group made the experimental discovery in 2018 with Cao and colleagues. The theory-plus-experiment configuration is clean, though the junior experimentalist Yuan Cao is not in the supplied names and cannot be proposed.
assessment.maturity: Strongly reproduced across many groups within a few years, but the nature of the superconducting pairing is still debated, so the interpretation is not fully stable. Somewhat early but defensible.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity is unresolved.
Whether recognition is premature compared with older, better-settled candidates; the roles of Cao and others are outside the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong coupling between a superconducting qubit and a microwave resonator controllable and became the architecture for superconducting quantum processors and quantum-limited readout. Clear concept with decisive experiments and an enormous impact on quantum technology. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which makes this a natural follow-on.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf proposed cQED in 2004 and Wallraff et al. demonstrated strong coupling the same year. The credit has four or five core contributors; picking Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Girvin is one reasonable trio, with Blais left out as a plausible injustice.
assessment.maturity: Replicated across many labs, with dispersive readout, gates and error-correction experiments built on it. The platform is mature though the larger computing promise is not yet realised.
uncertainties: Which of the theory or experiment contributors would be omitted, and whether the 2025 prize reduces appetite for another circuit prize so soon.
Possible contribution overlap with the early Yale and Saclay/Delft qubit work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, enabling Mott-insulator transitions, quantum gas microscopy and probes of many-body dynamics. Original and widely consequential, bridging atomic physics and condensed matter. Direct overlap with my own area of quantum optics, so I treat it carefully.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and colleagues proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner, Bloch and Hänsch observed the superfluid-Mott transition in 2002; Bloch and Greiner later developed gas microscopy. Cirac is also credited; limiting to three means choosing between Cirac and Zoller, and the actual prize may be seen as split between theory and experiment.
assessment.maturity: Highly reproducible and extended to fermions and gauge-field settings, though the main payoff of quantum simulation beyond classical tractability is still being shown. The BEC prize (2001) and optical-lattice precision work lie nearby.
uncertainties: Allocation of credit between theory proposers and experimentalists, and overlap with the 2001 BEC and 2012 prizes.
Whether actual quantum advantage in simulation has been decisively demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution, starting with BB84, converted the no-cloning and measurement-disturbance principles into a practical security concept. It is conceptually elegant and links foundations to technology. The 2022 prize for entanglement tests lowers novelty somewhat.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard authored BB84; Ekert's entanglement-based protocol is a distinct contribution. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is another priority issue. Two laureates are the cleanest configuration, though leaving Ekert out would be contested.
assessment.maturity: Commercial and satellite QKD exist, but practical security (side channels, device independence) is still evolving, and the physics impact is arguably mostly conceptual.
uncertainties: Priority questions involving Wiesner and Ekert, and whether the topic falls more within computer science or physics.
Practical deployment limits and ongoing security loopholes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond created a room-temperature solid-state quantum sensor for magnetic fields, temperature and nanoscale NMR. This ties directly to the idea that progress depends on what can be measured and how precisely, and it fits my crystal-defect and spin-coherence background.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko achieved single-NV optical detection and spin control; Lukin and others pushed to nanoscale sensing, quantum registers and entanglement. Other contributors (Hanson, Awschalom, Yacoby, Hollenberg) make the three-name configuration contestable.
assessment.maturity: Replicated widely and with real applications emerging, but sensing sensitivity records and practical advantage over classical sensors are still maturing.
uncertainties: Whether the supplied three names capture the decisive contributions given Hanson, Awschalom and others.
Overlap with Lukin's other candidacies and uncertain commercial impact.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade supplies strong controllable interactions between neutral atoms, now enabling programmable tweezer arrays used for quantum simulation and gates. Rapidly influential and original, with a direct atomic-physics link.
assessment.attribution: Saffman, Lukin and coworkers proposed blockade-based gates; Browaeys and Grangier demonstrated blockade of single atoms and later arrays; Lukin's Harvard group led programmable arrays. Grangier is a fourth credit I cannot include. Tweezer-array contributions of Browaeys, Lukin, Bernien and others make allocation unclear.
assessment.maturity: Strong momentum and replication but still developing, with error-corrected computation only emerging; arguably premature.
uncertainties: Premature relative to other quantum-technology candidates and unclear credit for the arrays versus the blockade concept.
